about: Game UI rules this tool checks or hands to the implementer. Distilled from the November 2026 research brief on game UX/UI. The two Xbox pages were re-read on the checked date; the other sources are cited as the brief gives them and were not re-read here.

tiers.platform: a number a platform holder publishes; label: concern
tiers.normative: a published accessibility standard; label: failure
tiers.house: this tool's own rule, so a coding agent can read the design; label: deviation

checks.lint: worked out from the design before anything is built
checks.godot: measured in the running scene by tests/godot_ux_check.gd
checks.build: the design cannot show it; the implementer must build it
checks.human: a judgment a person makes; listed for review, never auto-decided

rules.title: Text is at least the platform minimum, measured as rendered body height
rules.detail: Console 26 px at 1080p (52 at 4K). PC 18 px at 1080p (36 at 4K). Handheld 17 pt body text. Body height is the pixel distance from the lowest descender to the highest ascender, not the font size.
rules.source: Xbox Accessibility Guideline 101 (re-read 2026-11-11); Apple, Designing for games

rules.title: Players can resize text up to 200% without losing content
rules.detail: Drive every size from one Theme and build layouts from containers so larger text reflows instead of clipping.

rules.title: Text contrast is at least 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text
rules.detail: Worked out per theme mode from the text color and the fill behind it.
rules.source: WCAG 2.x 1.4.3, as cited in Unity's accessibility guidance

rules.title: On a TV, text and controls stay inside the title-safe area
rules.detail: The inner 90% of the screen. Xbox's page gives 3456 x 1944 at 4K (exactly 90%) but 1720 x 1000 with 96 px and 40 px margins at 1080p, which do not agree with each other; this tool uses 5% on every side, which satisfies both.
rules.source: Xbox, Screen areas (re-read 2026-11-11); Amazon Fire TV design guidelines

rules.title: On a phone, ask the device for its safe area at run time
rules.detail: Notches, rounded corners and home indicators differ by device. Never hard-code insets.

rules.title: On touch screens, anything tappable is at least 44 by 44 points
rules.detail: 48 by 48 dp when the frame is tagged for Android.
rules.source: Apple, Designing for games; Material Design 3 (Android figure, from the figma-appdesigner rulebook)

rules.title: Something has focus when a screen opens
rules.detail: Without initial focus, controller input does nothing. Tag one control [focus=first].
rules.source: Godot docs, Keyboard/Controller Navigation and Focus; research brief, Part 8

rules.title: Every control can be reached with directional input
rules.detail: The focus graph is explicit: neighbors come from [up=] [down=] [left=] [right=] tags, or are generated from layout and flagged for review.
rules.source: Godot docs, Keyboard/Controller Navigation and Focus; research brief, Part 8

rules.title: Every interactive component has a visible focus state
rules.detail: A focus state is not a hover state: hover does not exist on a gamepad. Checked when the export lists the component's states.

rules.title: Button prompts match the device in the player's hands
rules.detail: Tag a prompt [prompt=accept] instead of writing a button's name into the text. The implementer swaps the glyph when the input device changes.

rules.title: A destructive action is confirmed or can be undone
rules.detail: Error prevention belongs in menus, saves and shops, never in the designed challenge. Tag the control [confirm=<screen or dialog>] or [undo=yes].
rules.source: Hodent, The Gamer's Brain (error prevention and recovery)

rules.title: The same action has the same label everywhere
rules.detail: Checked across screens by action id.

rules.title: Every interactive control names the action it triggers
rules.detail: [action=start_game]. Without it a coding agent has a button and no verb.

rules.title: Layers are named for what they are
rules.detail: A layer still called Frame 12 or Rectangle 3 tells an implementer nothing and becomes a node with that name.

rules.title: Visible text has a string key
rules.detail: [key=menu.play]. Keys go to figma/strings.csv for translation; text with no key gets a generated one, flagged.

rules.title: Colors are variables, not loose hex values
rules.detail: A bound color becomes a theme entry and changes with the mode. A loose one is frozen.

rules.title: Menus use auto layout; only a HUD is positioned by hand
rules.detail: Hand-placed controls become brittle pixel offsets. Tag an overlay frame [kind=hud] to say the placement is deliberate.

rules.title: No information is conveyed by color alone
No flickering images or repetitive patterns
All settings are saved
Controls can be remapped
All important speech is subtitled, with size and background options
rules.detail: No more than 38 characters per line.
rules.source: Game Accessibility Guidelines, Basic; IGDA Game Accessibility SIG top ten

rules.title: Screen shake, flashes and motion blur can be turned down or off
rules.detail: Juice reliably improves appeal; whether it helps understanding depends on context. If an effect carries information, test it as information.

rules.title: Every interaction shows what can be done and what just happened
rules.source: Hodent, The Gamer's Brain (signs and feedback)

rules.title: Each system is marked as intended challenge or as interface
rules.detail: The usability rules apply to the interface. They do not apply to what is meant to be hard.

rules.title: Each piece of HUD information has a chosen register
rules.detail: Diegetic, meta, spatial or plain HUD. Tag it [register=hud]. Diegesis is a tool, not a goal.
rules.source: Fagerholt and Lorentzon, Beyond the HUD (2009)

rules.title: Teach one new thing at a time, by doing, and let experts skip
Reference libraries keep their owners' terms
rules.detail: The Game UI Database's creator has said its content may not be used for anything related to machine learning. Keep it as a human reference and out of any agent's inputs.
